messages.subject: [S] principal components on leptokurtotic data
messages.body_plain:
Dear Readers,
For those who care, I've compiled the replies to my initial question
regarding
principal components on leptokurtotic data.
Regards,

Matthew A. Kurbat, Ph.D.

Phone:  704 - 386 - 6690
Fax:            704 - 386 - 1175

ORIGINAL POSTING
>
>
>Dear Readers,
>
>I wish to perform principal components analysis on leptokurtotic data.
>
>Because the data are not multivariate normal, uncorrelated principal
>components do not imply independent components, which
>is a problem for my particular application.
>
>Does anyone know of a reference or references on some appropriate
>generalization of the correlation/covariance matrix 
>that might solve this problem (or any other way to solve it?).
>
>Thank you very much,
>

REPLIES

Nonlinear principal components, with automatic transformation of variables
to achieve maximum redundancy, may help.  See the transcan function in
the S-Plus Hmisc library (see web address below or use StatLib).
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Department of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

Matthew,
    As you probably know pca can be and often is applied whether or
not data are multivariate normal....not even to a close approximation.
Two quick options you might try:
1.  Transform each column to RANKS (apply(x,2,rank) is quick) and see
    if the correlational structure makes sense, despite having thrown  
    away a good deal of the information (but not the order info.).
2.  Try various forms of Box-Cox transformations on the respective variates,
    individually, seeking to achieve 'decent looking' pairwise plots.
Both alternatives fail to deal with many aspects of your problem, but then
no PCA methodolology will, w/out further elaboration.  
    I have worked on this sort of problem for some time, and believe there
is not too much sound guidance in the literature.  If you care to elaborate
a little on your problem I might be able to help (But I'm off for a 3 week
trip on thurs. so ...)
    Best regards,
     Bob Pruzek
     Professor, Statistics 
     SPH, SUNY, Albany

This query probably cannot be answered without further detailed information
about the intended goal of the statistical analysis.  And even then,
there may be some difficulties!  Linear principal components analysis
accomplishes (at least) two conceptually unrelated goals simultaneously:
(1)  It gives a sequence of normalized linear functions of the data each of
which has maximum variance, subject to being uncorrelated with the
preceeding
terms, and  (2)  It provides variables in the correct order to allow
(linear)
reconstruction of the data with smallest sum of squared errors using the
fewest
possible terms.  It is a bonus that under normality the components are
also strictly independent.
 
If actual independence of the `principal' components becomes the goal, then
one must move over to nonlinear principal components methods, and then one
must
decide whether the goal is  (1)  or  (2)  as stated above.  There is no
generalization of the covariance matrix that will lead to independence in
general.
The current state of these issues is probably best summarized in the paper
by
Salinelli in the 1998 Annals of Statistics, pages 596-616.  This paper is
quite mathematical and therefore hard to read, but it does contain some
relevant references.  Note that if attaining independence really is the
goal,
the curse of dimensionality will be particularly severe!
 
Hope this helps some?
 
Andrey Feuerverger / University of Toronto

There are interesting papers published recently about an alternative
measures of dependence that work for non-Gaussian variables (most of these
measures have been known for a long time, though). One of the most fresh is

messages.subject: [S] Robusticity in Discriminant [not just S]
messages.body_plain:
Warning:  this is not exclusively an S question.

Suppose I am interested in classifying objects into groups.  This, of
course, is the typical problem for which linear (multiple) discriminant
analysis was developed.  In the past 20 or so years, other techniques that
are less dependent on normality and distributional assumptions have
appeared -- multiple logistic regression, tree-based classifiers, neural
networks, for example.

Here is my problem:

Suppose I have a 10 group classification problem.  Each group is scored for
15 continuous variables.  The group sizes vary from 15 at the low end to
120 at the high end, with a fairly wide range of sizes in between.  Some of
the variables appear to be normal (both within the groups and for the whole
sample), while others appear to be quite skewed (some positive, some
negative).  The degree of skewing depends on the groups themselves.  In
some groups it is positive while in others it is negative.  The covariance
matrices are not homogeneous either.  There are also outliers in many
groups, but the outliers are not unexpected -- these are biological
populations and there *are* outliers.  The sampling itself is opportunistic
-- we take what we can get from the museums that curate this material.  As
long as it is adult and shows no obvious signs of skeletal pathology we use
it.  Eliminated outliers simply because they are outliers is not an option.

In other words, virtually all the assumptions upon which LDA is based seem
to be violated in this data set.

Despite this, LDA gives very high classification accuracy both with the
training sets and the test sets of data.  One author claims that if you get
high classification accuracy in these circumstances, to heck with the
assumptions.

What I'm trying to decide is "when"  and "why" I should consider some of
the alternative techniques.  

To bring this back to S for a moment, the VR2 function lda() offers a
number of options for constructing the within covariance matrix -- moment
(the default), mve, mle, t).   It doesn't seem to matter which of these
techniques I use.  The classification accuracy doesn't change much.

SAS offers a fairly wide variety of kernel density estimators for
non-parametric discriminant analysis.  

And, of course, there are routines like RPART and multinom(), which are
infinitely more complicated to interpret with data like this, but still
give fairly reasonable prediction accuracy.

The bottom line for me is whether or not one should just "chuck" these
alternative techniques for classification whenever plain, ordinary, lda
gives reliable results even if the face of gross violations of its assumptions.

Any of your wise counsel would be appreciated.

Marc Feldesman

Dr. Marc R. Feldesman
email:  feldesmanm at pdx.edu
email:  feldesman at ibm.net
fax:    503-725-3905

"Math is hard.  Let's go to the mall"  Barbie

On Sun, 14 Mar 1999, Marc R. Feldesman wrote:

> 
> Warning:  this is not exclusively an S question.
> 
> Suppose I am interested in classifying objects into groups.  This, of
> course, is the typical problem for which linear (multiple) discriminant
> analysis was developed.  In the past 20 or so years, other techniques that
> are less dependent on normality and distributional assumptions have
> appeared -- multiple logistic regression, tree-based classifiers, neural
> networks, for example.
> 
> Here is my problem:
> 
> Suppose I have a 10 group classification problem.  Each group is scored for
> 15 continuous variables.  The group sizes vary from 15 at the low end to
> 120 at the high end, with a fairly wide range of sizes in between.  Some of
> the variables appear to be normal (both within the groups and for the whole
> sample), while others appear to be quite skewed (some positive, some
> negative).  The degree of skewing depends on the groups themselves.  In
> some groups it is positive while in others it is negative.  The covariance
> matrices are not homogeneous either.  There are also outliers in many
> groups, but the outliers are not unexpected -- these are biological
> populations and there *are* outliers.  The sampling itself is opportunistic
> -- we take what we can get from the museums that curate this material.  As
> long as it is adult and shows no obvious signs of skeletal pathology we use
> it.  Eliminated outliers simply because they are outliers is not an option.
> 
> In other words, virtually all the assumptions upon which LDA is based seem
> to be violated in this data set.

However, most of them are not that important, unless you want
posterior probabilities when LDA can be highly over-confident.

> Despite this, LDA gives very high classification accuracy both with the
> training sets and the test sets of data.  One author claims that if you get
> high classification accuracy in these circumstances, to heck with the
> assumptions.

I would do almost all the way with that. My caveat would be if such small
groups are really representative: a new observation might be quite
different, and LDA could be confident while badly wrong.

> What I'm trying to decide is "when"  and "why" I should consider some of
> the alternative techniques.  
> 
> To bring this back to S for a moment, the VR2 function lda() offers a
> number of options for constructing the within covariance matrix -- moment
> (the default), mve, mle, t).   It doesn't seem to matter which of these
> techniques I use.  The classification accuracy doesn't change much.

Nope, but the posterior probs might.

> SAS offers a fairly wide variety of kernel density estimators for
> non-parametric discriminant analysis.  

I certainly would not use that in more that a very small number of 
dimensions (3 or 4).

> And, of course, there are routines like RPART and multinom(), which are
> infinitely more complicated to interpret with data like this, but still
> give fairly reasonable prediction accuracy.

Why is multinom more complicated?  Like LDA it gives g-1 linear combination
of the variables, of which you choose the largest, and you convert them to
prosterior probabilities in the same way. You cna think of it as just
another way to fit LDA, one that is known to be more robust still, but a
little less efficient were LDA's assumptions right.

I _would_ use multiple logistic regression.  Now, multinom is not the most
efficient way possible to fit it, but it is there and ought to do
your task.  I think MLR is a technique that has been scandalously
under-represented in the statistical textbooks: all the (de)merits
have been known for at least a couple of decades.

--

messages.subject: RE: [S] Robusticity in Discriminant [not just S]
messages.body_plain:
Your suggestions on MLR and multinom interest me greatly. I use discriminant 
analysis primarily to find those dimensions (axes) in the multivariate data 
space which maximally separate known biological subgroupings. I would typically 
use graphical means to assess visually how much separation or overlap there is 
between groups along those dimensions, and interpret the loadings of the 
original variables on those dimensions to interpret the biological meaning of 
those separations. I understand that for such purposes LDA  is fairly robust 
against departures of normality and similarity of the within-group covariance 
matrices. However, the data I'm currently working with is **very** 
non-normal...  I am not familiar with MLR and would be very interested to know 
if it would be useful for my purposes. Any pointers or references appreciated.

Willem de Winter
Dept of Anatomy and Human Biology
University of Western Australia

messages.subject: [S] Bugs in Menu Versions of Two Sample t-test and Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test
messages.subject_clean: [S] Bugs in Menu Versions of Two Sample t-test and Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Sorry if this has already been posted.  I'm using S-PLUS for Windows 
Version 4.5, Release 2.

The menu versions of the two-sample t-test and Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test 
give incorrect results if you use grouping by a variable and specify a 
one-sided alternative hypothesis.  For example,

     dum.df1 <- data.frame(data = 1:6, group = c(rep("a", 3), 
rep("b",3)))

     dum.df2 <- data.frame(data = 1:6, group = c(rep("b", 3), 
rep("a",3)))

If you set the Response Variable to data and the Grouping Variable to 
group, and specify "greater" for the alternative hypothesis, you get 
the same results for both of the above data frames.  The function that 
is being called always identifies the data in "x" with the factor level 
that comes first.

Sincerely,

--Steve M.

messages.subject: RE: [S] interval censoring in survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
About ten days ago, Mark Stevenson posted a request for information on interval 
censored data.
Unfortunately, I was not able to reply before he sent a summary of the 
responses to the s-news mailing list.
Therefore, I send my reply to the mailing list directly.

Of the references mentioned, I only know the books by Klein and Moeschberger 
(1997), Andersen, Borgan, Gill, Keiding (1993) and Collett (1994).
Indeed, all these books at least introduce the concept of interval censored 
data, and Klein and Moeschberger and Collett also pay some attention to 
estimation issues. However, it is quite surprising that some important 
references have not been mentioned. The best source of information on interval 
censored data that I know of can be found in
@INPROCEEDINGS{Groe:96,
        author = {Piet Groeneboom},
        title = {Lectures on inverse problems},
        booktitle = {Lectures on probability theory, Ecole d'Et\'e de 
Probabilit\'es de {Saint-Flour XXIV-1994}},
        editor = {P. Bernard}, 
        publisher = {Springer Verlag, Berlin},
        year = 1996}
One chapter is devoted to computational issues, explaining why Turnbull's 
EM-algorithm is not the best approach. In the last chapter, asymptotics of the 
NPMLE are discussed. It shows that standard asymptotic theory does not hold, 
and thus the use of the Fisher information matrix to obtain standard errors can 
not be justified by asymptotic considerations.  In Turnbull's paper 
Nonparametric estimation of a survivorship function with doubly censored data 
(JASA,1974)such asymptotics are discussed. He correctly states that it only 
holds if the number of time points (m) remains fixed and that " a more 
interesting problem is the one of consistency when m \rightarrow \infty and the 
widths of the intervals become arbitrarily small -- it is hoped to treat this 
case in a later paper". The above reference and a book by Groeneboom and 
Wellner 
@BOOK{GrWe:92,
        author = {Piet Groeneboom and Jon A. Wellner},
        title = {Information bounds and nonparametric maximum likelihood 
estimation},
        publisher = {Birkh\"{a}user Verlag},
        year = 1992
}
can be seen as this later paper, indicating that asymptotics with interval 
censored data are much more difficult than with right censored data.
Note that Klein/Moeschberger refer to this approach, but do not mention the 
assumption of the number of time points held fixed! The kaplanMeier function in 
S-PLUS 4.5 (see below) also claims to compute standard errors via this approach.

S-PLUS 4.5 for windows has Turnbull's algorithm incorporated, through a 
function called kaplanMeier (which I think is a misleading name, since the 
NPMLE for interval censored data has little to do with the Kaplan-Meier 
approach). I compared kaplanMeier with the program written by Groeneboom for 
data on HIV-seroconversion from the Amsterdam cohort studies on HIV infection 
and AIDS. The results are in the attached postscript file. In principle, both 
approaches should yield similar results, which is not the case. I tend to have 
more confidence in the program by Groeneboom (however, I may be biased, since 
he was my Ph.D. supervisor). At least, my output from kaplanMeier is somewhat 
strange (look at the intervals): 

                              Survival
        (    -Inf, 1982.034]    1.000
        (1982.163, 1982.645]    0.961
        (1982.782, 1982.935]    0.913
        (1983.302, 1983.335]    0.913
        (1983.466, 1984.772]    0.913
        (1984.947, 1985.216]    0.884
        (1985.413, 1985.785]    0.819
        (1985.938, 1986.021]    0.814
        (1986.149, 1986.168]    0.814
        (1986.289, 1986.193]    0.814
        (1986.322, 1986.231]    0.814

 

More information and papers on interval censored data can be found at the site
   http://www.stat.washington.edu/jaw/RESEARCH/PAPERS/available.html

I especially recommend

Interval Censored Survival Data: A Review of Recent Progress. Jian Huang and 
Jon A. Wellner. In: Proceedings of the First Seattle Symposium in 
Biostatistics, D. Y. Lin and T. R. Fleming, editors. Lecture Notes in 
Statistics 123, 123 - 170. 
Huang, J. (1996). Efficient Estimation for the Cox Model with Interval 
Censoring. Annals of Statistics 24, 540-568. 
Efficient Estimation for the Proportional Hazards Model with ``Case 2'' 
Interval Censoring. Jian Huang and Jon A. Wellner. Submitted to Biometrika , 
May, 1995. Technical Report 290, May 1995

A program for interval censored data can be downloaded from
  http://www.stat.washington.edu/jaw/RESEARCH/SOFTWARE/software.list.html
Unfortunately, only a Macintosh version is available at the moment.

Ronald Geskus

I would do it like this:

datframename[, "x2"]_ifelse(dataframename[, "x1"]==1 & dataframename[,
"id"]==1, 1, dataframename[, "x2"])

essentially, this says if the dataframe columns  "x1" and "id" equal 1 to
rewrite column x2 with a 1, otherwise return the value of the column x2.
It's a little easier when the data are in arrays and vectors.
Alternatively, you could make a new vector and bind it onto the data frame.

I hope this helps, 

Tim

messages.subject: Re: [S] interval censoring in survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "GR" == Geskus, Ronald <rgeskus at gggd.amsterdam.nl> writes:

    GR> Efficient Estimation for the Proportional Hazards Model with
    GR> ``Case 2'' Interval Censoring. Jian Huang and Jon
    GR> A. Wellner. Submitted to Biometrika , May, 1995. Technical
    GR> Report 290, May 1995

I've written the software for this SPMLE (or NPMLE).  The caveat is
that it requires one to find a decent freely available nonlinear
programming optimizer.  I used CFSQP, but it's not freely
redistributable (and one must get a license for commercial use).

It uses either a convex minorant algorithm and profiling, or nonlinear
programming.  NLP performs a bit better and seems to be marginally
safer with respect to starting values.

The best approach I think would be EM for initial values, profiling to
get into the neighborhood of the optimum, and NLP to reach the top
quickly.

2 other caveats:
        - it needs a good bit of cleaning, and a small bit of generalizing. 
        - starting values need to be carefully chosen (there are a
          number of papers in the literature whose results on IC data
          (not simulated data) are flat out wrong because they didn't
          worry enough about the numerical results/starting values
          (and large parameter problems have likelihoods which can
          look "flat-enough" away from the optimum).

best,
-tony

messages.subject_clean: [S] LU - QR - SVD problem in Matrix library
messages.body_plain:
I have encountered a problem using the lu, qr, and svd
decompositions in the Matrix library. I use each of these
methods to solve for the coefficients of the Longley data
(Longley, JASA, 1967).  I compare each method's solution
to the certified values provided by the NIST StRD
(http://www.nist.gov/itl/div898/strd).  The lu gives about
eight digits of accuracy, which is what I expected.
However, the qr and svd each yield about two digits of
accuracy.  I had expected that the qr would be more accurate
than the lu, and in turn, that the svd would be more accurate
than the qr.  Invoking the "pivot=T" option for qr improved
the results very marginally.  Changing lu.Matrix() to lu()
and solve.lu.Matrix() to solve() had no effect.

I also observe that the help file for lu.Matrix uses
the command "lu.Matrix(x)" in the examples, whereas
the example for qr.Matrix uses "qr(A,pivot=T)" rather
than the expected "qr.Matrix(A,pivot=T)" and similarly,
the example for svd.Matrix uses "svd(A)" rather than
the expected "svd.Matrix(A)".

I am running S-PLUS v4.5 release 2 on a 300MHz Pentium under
Windows98.  Attached please find a script file which scans
in the data, sets up and executes the decompositions, and
counts the number of accurate digits.  I have commented the
code, and apologize for its lack of elegance.

Please reply to me directly. I will summarize comments
for the list.

messages.subject: Re: [S] interval censoring in survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
A few people have mentioned various references to
approaches to the interval censoring problem.

None have mentined the two articles with almost identical content appeared in 
Statistics in Medicine in 1996:

CP Farrington: Interval censored survival data: A generalized linear
modelling approach
Stat. Med 15, pp. 283-2929, 1996

B Carstensen: Regression models for interval censored data: Application to
HIV infection
in Danish Homosexual men. Stat. Med. 15, pp. 2177-2189, 1996

These papers give a very simple way of dealing with interval censored
survival data.
The only reqirement is ability to fit slightliy non-standard generalized
linear models.
Easy in S or R or GLIM(!). And of course data. Both papers assume a
piecewise constant
underlying hazard, which is a problem if data is scarce, so the papers are
only of 
interest for people who actually have data to anlyse.

Bendix

messages.subject: [S] class, oldClass, S 4, S+ 5
messages.body_plain:
I am just starting to modify my S-Plus libraries to work under S-Plus 5.x.
As the maintainer of source code to hundreds of functions (using Emacs
and S-mode under ESS, not through .Data) I am disappointed that
John Chambers preempted the use of 'class' for S version 4.  I can see
no reason why the new meaning of 'class' could not be called 'Class',
and the old meaning remain under the same name 'class' instead of
'oldClass'.  As the new 'class' is quite restrictive for objects as flexible
and fluid as model fit objects, I will need to make hundreds of changes
to my source code.  Coupled with the fact that I want the same source
code to be downward compatible back to S-Plus version 3.4. 

I cannot merely override the definition of class(x) and 'class<-' as
this would conflict with the use of S-Plus version 5 functions that will
be relying on the new 'class'.  I have another problem that I often
take the following short cut in returning objects in a function:

   structure(list(object parts), attribute1='xxxxx', class='y')

instead of w <- structure(list(object parts), attribute1='xxxxx')
                  class(w) <- 'y'
                  w

It would be nice of MathSoft had a simple solution that would not
require an amazing amount of editing (thank goodness for Emacs
at least), that maintains downward compatibility.  I haven't
used version 5 to see how the conversion utilities work but again
I don't want to maintain two sets of source code.

I wonder if other users are as irritated as I on the change of definition
of 'class'.

Thanks,

Frank Harrell

messages.subject: [S] class and oldclass
messages.body_plain:
I'll let John C defend himself about the "why" of the change, but please
note that the original beta-versions did not have the dichotomy.  It was
assumed that a single "class" function could be written that was smart enough
to handle both the new and old cases, but that didn't work out.  Perfect
prescience is preternaturally rare.

  For the survival routines I made the following changes.  I also maintain 
these outside of S (using SCCS) so the automatic conversions offered are not
appropriate.
        1. First goal: a single source code that would work for both version
Splus5 and Splus4.  I use the Splus5 style as my main one.

        2. I had to remove the few "structure(... ,class='whatever')" calls
luckily there were only 2.

        3. Four routines had inheritance: coxph.null from coxph, survexp
from survfit, survfit.cox from survfit and survreg.penal from survreg.
For each of these a line was added to the appropriate routine, e.g.,
        setOldClass('survfit.cox', 'survfit')
to the top of surfit.coxph.s. 

        4. All "class(x) <- ..." were changed to "oldClass".  For the four
routines with inheritance, the right hand side is a single class rather
than a vector.  I did this with a shell script and sed -- about 1/2 hour
of fiddling and checking + 5 min to actually do it for 97 functions.

        5. My makefile for version4 pulls all .s functions through the following
sed script.  (For non Unix folks, sed is a batch mode editor and occassionally
quite useful).  The first and last lines of the script handle almost all the
cases, the middle lines restore the proper line for the 4 special routines.
(s is the substitute command, " *" is one or more spaces and ['"] is either
single or double quote).

/setOldClass/d
s/oldClass(fit) *<- *fit$method\[1]/class(fit) <- fit$method/
s/oldClass(out) *<- *['"]survexp['"]/class(out) <- c('survexp', 'survfit')/
s/oldClass(temp) *<- *['"]survfit.cox['"]/class(temp) <- c('survfit.cox', 'survf
it')/
s/oldClass(fit) *<- *['"]survreg.penal['"]/class(fit)<- c('survreg.penal', 'surv
reg')/
s/oldClass(/class(/

        6. The setInterface calls are all in a separate file, which is
not included in the 3.x or 4.x source.

  I emphatically agree that you do not want to try to translate the old
class style to the new one, which is far too restrictive for the object
resulting from a model fit.  

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: [S] Measures of Fit for GLM - AIC, BIC, etc?
messages.subject_clean: [S] Measures of Fit for GLM - AIC, BIC, etc?
messages.body_plain:
For the massive health data sets we have available here, I and my
research staff periodically develop GLM models to examine relationships
between emergency room visits or hospital admissions for asthma and
several independent variables & factors (Poisson GLM); or between cost
of health care per insured person and possible predictors (Gamma GLM or
Tweedie GLM). 

I am interested in methods for measure-based testing of the adequacy and
fit of these GLM models for these different probability distributions.

I have relied somewhat on the built-in AIC measures of current and
extended (Venables & Ripley) SPlus routines. But there seems to be a
subtle debate about which implementation of AIC is better (am I stating
this right?): viz. some older snews discussion regarding Trevor Hastie,
Pregibon  or others' earlier work incorporated in the standard S-Plus
GLM routines as the basis for stopping rules and deciding better fit,
versus some later measures as suggested in the V&R MASS enhancement.

I am looking for an explicit statement or discussion of SPlus
algorithmic implementations of AIC (ok I'll even allow BIC here) for
different probability models.

Has anyone systematically looked at AIC and how its should be / could
optionally be specified as S-Plus functions for DIFFERENT KINDS of
probability distribution assumptions, namely Poisson, Gamma, and hey
let's thrwo in the curve ball here: even Tweedie models ?

Thanks for any assistance with this request.
Aloha from Hawaii (but it's cloudy & raining today..)
Andy White

messages.subject: RE: [S] class, oldClass, S 4, S+ 5
messages.body_plain:
Fellow splussers,

if Terry Therneau and Frank Harrell are finding so much frustration
converting to S4, what chance do I have?

I'm intrigued by the comments about "objects as flexible and fluid as
model fit objects". I thought non-flexible, properly pre-planned classes
was a feature? If you don't know what a collection is going to contain,
just make it a list? If you find you need to add some more members,
design a derived class?

I suspect the real problem is that object orientation was just an add-on
in S3; it takes us aback when we're forced to use it properly as in S4.
Not that this helps convert from one to the other, of course. Is there
really no way of programming a working auto-conversion even if it is
horrible? I'm thinking of converting old classes back to pure named
lists and checking for autoconversion of function() to explicit
function.method(), using function overloading only for new classes, at
least until I get round to re-writing properly. (Given that I've
somewhat publicly vowed only to use R, this may take some time ...)

But then, I don't have a problem on anything like the same scale as TT
and FH. My deepest sympathies to them and anyone else fighting the good
fight.

Simon Fear

messages.subject: [S] survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
S-plusers,

I had such a good response to my last question that I thought I'd try you
all with another (probably more philosophical) query.

In veterinary epidemiology we're often interested in time to event data e.g.
the number of days between when a cow enters a herd and when she exits
(either on the back of a truck or into a hole in the ground).

One favourite analysis at the moment is to use survival analysis to look at
conception rates. Dairy cows are mated at each heat after calving until they
conceive. Usually this means each individual will receive anywhere between
1 - 5 matings.

Some of our colleagues have used survival analysis to look at the proportion
of a group of cows conceiving at each mating  (time = mating number, event
of interest = conception).

My question for you is: is it valid to use a survival analysis approach when
you have only series of discrete (in this example up to 5) "times" when the
event can occur? Would logistic regression be more appropriate for this type
of analysis?

Whats the feeling from the experts?

Mark S.

messages.subject: Re: [S] survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
My only comment is that logistic regression would not be appropriate unless
all observation times are equal. The fact that the Cox model explicitly
incorporates different follow up times makes it better when this is an
issue.  For a good simple discussion of the Cox model and survival analysis
and when/where it may not be appropriate, see Kleinbaum's "Survival
Analysis" .  I don't see any reason why only having 5 "times" would make
the Cox model inappropriate or why that would make logistic regression more
preferable.

Tim

messages.subject_clean: [S] subsetting a data frame with multiple measurement
messages.body_plain:
Renaud Lancelot <lancelot at telecomplus.sn> wrote:

>> Dear S-Plus users,
>> 
>> I have a data frame with multiple measurements, i.e.
>> measurements are repeated at different occasions on
>> the same id. I want to select the lines for which id
>> appears at least n times. How should I do ?
>>
>> ...

Use one of the following functions (and see the example below)

select1 <- function(id, n){
  z <- as.variable(factor(id, labels=table(id)))
  z>=n
}

select2 <- function(id, n){
  ord <- order(id)
  r <- rle(id[ord])$lengths
  z <- rep(r, r)
  z[ord] <- z
  z>=n
}

Example: data frame 'fuel.frame'
-------
  
> summary(fuel.frame)

       Fuel            Type

 Median :4.348   Medium :13  
 Mean   :4.210   Small  :13

Select all rows in 'fuel.frame' for which the levels of the

X <- fuel.frame[select1(fuel.frame$Type, 10), ]

messages.subject: [S] Summary: subsetting a data frame with multiple measurement
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: subsetting a data frame with multiple measurement
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

Here is a summary of the replies I got from this query:

> I have a data frame with multiple measurements, i.e. measurements are
> repeated at different occasions on the same id. I want to select the
> lines for which id appears at least n times. How should I do ?
> To clarify (I guess...), I'd like something equivalent to the following
> SQL query
> SELECT DISTINCT * FROM Data WHERE id IN 
> (SELECT DISTINCT id FROM Data HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY id)

Many thanks to Jean Adams, Bill Dunlap, Terry Elrod, Christian Keller,
Dave Krantz and Andrew Sinclair for their accurate and very useful
answers. I also added a solution I had found in the meantime.

Best regards,

Renaud

################################################
### Solution from Bill Dunlap

counts <- function(x){
        x <- as.factor(x)
        tx <- table(x)
        tx[as.numeric(x)]
        }
x <- data.frame(id = c("One","Two","One","Three","One","Three"),
                age = c(11,12,13,14,15,16))
counts(x$id)
y <- x[counts(x$id)>1,]

### You could then sort by id with
y[order(y$id),]

### or use split(y, y$id) to split it up into a distinct data frame for
each id.
split(y, y$id)

############################################ Solution from Christian
Keller
select1 <- function(id, n){
  z <- as.variable(factor(id, labels=table(id)))
  z >= n
  }

select2 <- function(id, n){
  ord <- order(id)
  r <- rle(id[ord])$lengths
  z <- rep(r, r)
  z[ord] <- z
  z>=n
  }

### Select all rows in x for which the levels of the variable id appears
at least 2 times. 

select1(x$id, 2)
select2(x$id, 2)

x[select1(x$id, 2), ]
x[select2(x$id, 2), ]

####################################### Solution from Jean Adams
# vector of unique ids
uniq.id <- sort(unique(x$id))
uniq.id

# lines of data frame for which id appears at least 5 times
x[is.element(x$id, uniq.id[table(x$id) >=2 ]), ]

#################################### Solution from Terry Elrod
.t          <- table(x$id)
.which      <- names(.t[.t >= 2])
.test.table <- outer(x$id, .which, "==")
.test.table
.rws        <- apply(.test.table, 1, sum) > 0
x[.rws,]

################################### Solution from Andrew Sinclair
### now identify which id numbers are wanted
reqd.ids <- sort(unique(x$id)) [ table(x$id) >= 2 ]

### use match() to locate the required ids within original data
final.answer <- x[!is.na(match(x$id , reqd.ids)),]
final.answer

### You may want to sort the final answer to see the groups together, eg
id.order <- order(final.answer$id)
final.answer[id.order,]

################################## Solution from Dave Krantz
x[!is.na(match(x$id, sort(unique(x$id))[table(x$id) >= 2])), ]

################################## Solution from Renaud Lancelot
x[is.element(x$id, names(table(x$id)[table(x$id) >= 2])), ]

-- 
Renaud Lancelot

BP 2057 Dakar-Hann
Senegal

messages.subject: [S] importing microsoft access sheets
messages.body_plain:
dear all
original question; how to import a microsoft access database by the
commandline:
thanks to among others: Renaud Lancelot, Pierre Delfosse, Nick Ellis,
Zhoorong Jiao, Chuck taylor, Willem J. Klokman, tim jones:
The answer was not so difficult:
use FileType="Access"   (instead of "mdb")
However, what I learned from the answers  as a general method, if you
want to mimmick something from the menu, just work with the menu and
open the log-file. Then the answer will present itself.
Strange enough using the logged command exactly in a function did work:

import.data(FileName = "H:\\tags\\x159r.MDB",
        FileType = "Access",
        ColNames = "",
        Format = "",
        TargetStartCol =  1,
        DataFrame = "x59r",
        NameRow = "",
        StartCol =  1,
        EndCol = "END",
        StartRow =  1,
        EndRow = "END",
        Delimiters = "\t",
        SeparateDelimiters = F,
        PageNumber =  1,
        RowNameCol = "",
        StringsAsFactors = "Auto",
        Filter = "",
        OdbcConnection = "",
        OdbcSqlQuery = "")

But replacing "H:\\tags\\x159r.MDB" by:
paste("H:\\tags\\",filename,sep="") did NOT!
with the following error:

Error -1 returned when opening data source 'H\tags\x159r.MDB' for
reading.
Internal error message was 'Cannot open Access File: H\tags\x159r.MDB'.

Many thanks so far!

messages.subject: RE: [S] Setting Default Files for Object Browser
messages.subject_clean: [S] Setting Default Files for Object Browser
messages.body_plain:
To S-News;

Re: My S-Plus default search directory issue.

Jack Lee's response below stimulated me to more carefully READ THE
PROGRAMMER'S MANUAL. I had already done what he describes, except I used the
S_DATA switch instead of the S_PROJ switch on my command line to avoid
having to copy my customized (made the default) S_Prefs directory for each
project. However, as Jack points out, S-Plus does this automatically and --
what I missed -- makes the driectory given the current working directory
(this can also be done with the S_CWD switch on the command line). This is
what makes S-Plus do exactly what I want. 

Another S-Plus arcanity demystified! Thanks Jack.

-- Bert

> ----------
> From:         Lee, Jack
> Sent:         Thursday, March 18, 1999 9:20 AM
> To:   Gunter, Bert
> Subject:      RE: [S] Setting Default Files for Object Browser
> 
> Dear Bert,
> 
> Assume that you have a new project called 'task1', the way I do is:
> 
> (1) create a subdirectory for the project, e.g. u:\task1
> (2) create an S-Plus data directory under task1, say, u:\task1\_data
> (3) make another copy of the Splus shortcut icon 
> (4) right click the new copy of the Splus shortcut icon
> (5) rename it to 'task1'
> (6) right click the task1 icon and choose property
> (7) click the 'Shortcut' tab
> (8) in the 'Target' field add: "C:\Program Files\splus45\cmd\SPLUS.EXE"
> S_PROJ=u:\task1
> (9) in the 'Start in' field type u:\task1
> (10) click OK
> (11) double click the task1 icon and you are in business.
> When you start Splus in task1 for the first time, Splus will prompt you to
> create the _prefs
> subdirectory for you. Just say OK. When you work on task1, the default
> directory will be u:\task1.
> I create one icon for each project I work on. I also have my slib
> subdirectory containing 
> my own functions. I have a .First() function to link to my slib
> automatically no matter where
> I start Splus. 
> 
> I hope this will help.
> 
> Jack
> 
> ____________________________________________________
> 
> J. Jack Lee, Ph.D.
> Associate Professor
> UTMDACC and Merck Research Laboratory
> lee at odin.mdacc.tmc.edu
> (732) 594-0475 (PHONE)
> (732) 594-6075 (FAX)

On Thu, 18 Mar 1999, Renaud Lancelot wrote:

> 
> Christian Keller and Dave Krantz asked me to outline that the
> is.element() function involved in 2 of the solutions is not available in
> 3.x versions of S-Plus. It is only available in 4.x / Windows and 5.x /
> Unix.

But easily added to a set of personal functions, and already revealed by
Bill V.:

Date: Sat, 11 Oct 1997 11:54:08 +0930
From: Bill Venables <wvenable at attunga.stats.adelaide.edu.au>
To: JOHN THADEN <JJTHADEN at life.uams.edu>
Cc: s-news at utstat.toronto.edu
Subject: Re: %in%

JOHN THADEN writes:

 > Recently, several functions contributed to s-news have made
 > use of a function %in%.  When I try to run subset.df, I get
 > the error
 > 
 > > contrasts(subset.df(a.df, fac!='p3'))
 > Error: couldn't find function "%in%"
 > Dumped
 > 
 > Is %in% in Splus, or is it in another library I should get?

It is in an unofficial library.  However S-PLUS 4.0 has an
equivalent function called is.element:

> is.element
function(el, set)
!is.na(match(el, set, nomatch = NA))

You use  is.element(elts, set)  instead of  (elts %in% set)

To my mind there are two reasons for sticking to the official
version: 

1. Using standard functions when available can only help
   portability of software.

2. There is already a use for %in% as a binary operator in linear
   model formulae and using it for something else can only foster
   confusion in the hearts of the young or innocent.

 > I am running Splus 3.4 under Win95.

Now I am really surprised.  Splus 3.4 was only released for Unix...

messages.subject: [S] steinhaus similarity coefficient
messages.body_plain:
Hello - 
I am trying to create a function which will incorporate the
Steinhaus similarity coefficient as the "metric= " arguement of the
generic dist function in Windows S-plus 4.5. I am creating
distance vectors for use in a Mantel test, and would like to use the 
Steinhaus coefficient as my ecological distance measure. The 
Steinhaus can be found in Legendre and Legendre (1998) 
Numerical Ecology, pp.265 and is described as follows:

S (x1,x2) =    2W/(A+B)

where W is the sum of the minimum abundances of the various 
species, A and B are the sums of the abundances of all species at 
each of the two sites being compared, i.e.:

                Species abundances      A       B       W
Site x1 7       3       0       0       10
Site x2 2       4       7       0               13
Minimum 2       3       0       0                       5

The function dist is not presented as a full program in the S-plus 4.5 
version, so I am unsure of its derivation. Is it possible to create a 
different "metric" for the function dist? Or, has anyone created an 
equivalent function for the Steinhaus coefficient to be used similarly 
to the dist function?
Thank you

Meg Krawchuk
Atlantic Cooperative Wildlife Ecology Research Network (ACWERN)
Biology Department
Acadia University
Wolfville N.S. BOP 1XO
meg.krawchuk at acadiau.ca

messages.subject: [S] Summary: routines for constrained minimisation without derivatives
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: routines for constrained minimisation without derivatives
messages.body_plain:
Here is my original question:

I'm looking for a (free) Fortran routine for function minimisation
without needing derivatives and allowing parameter constraints. This
routine is to be integrated in a S-Plus function for a bootstrap
procedure. I looked in Statlib and Netlib but I couldn't find any.

here are the answers I received (edited):

Matt Wiener: 
 Take a look at: FSQP Home Page:
http://www.isr.umd.edu/Labs/CACSE/FSQP/fsqp.html They don't charge, but
they do have some restrictions on use.  You'll have to see whether you
find them acceptable. 

Tom Richards:
 What about Nelder-Mead, discussed in Numerical Recipes?...(also
suggested by Samantha Choy and Kevin Brand)
 I don't know what type of constraints you're talking about exactly, but
if they're range constraints, you can just put in an if statement that
says, that if the parameters go outside the permissible range, then  the
function value will be arbitrarily large.

David Mackay: 
 Attached is a program you may find useful. This version came from
Michael Birnbaum's web site
http://psych.fullerton.edu/mbirnbaum/stepit.htm. There is a greatly
expanded version of stepit but I do not have it. The expanded version is
available, for a fee, from the Quantum Chemistry Program Exchange at
Indiana University http://qcpe5.chem.indiana.edu/qcpe.html. 

John Koval:
 I wrote an algorithm coded in Fortran which is in the Applied
statistics > library, known as AS319. think it is also available in
Statlib. I wrote it in Fortran 77, but someone coded it into Fortran 90.
It definitely works without derivatives, and can be made to handle
constraints by defining the function to have extremely large values when
> the constraints are violated - this is how I use it in one of my programs. 

Max Kuhn:
 The Nelder-Mead simplex routine code can be found in Statlib at:
http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/apstat/47 Also, the article Olsson, D. M.
(1774), A Sequential Simplex Program for Solving Minimization Problems.
Journal of Quality Technology, V 6, #1, pg 53 provides a Fortran
function list, as does the book Carter, W. H., Wampler, G. L. and
Stablein, D. L. (1983), Regression Analysis of Survival Data in Cancer
Chemotherapy. New York : Marcell Dekker . Also, there are some
interesting papers on this type of optimization routines (and others)
at: http://plato.la.asu.edu/guide.html (See the section for "M. Powell's
and M. Wright's papers on Direct Search methods"). 

Patrick Burns:
 There is already one in Splus called 'mnb0'.  See section 14.4 of 'S
Poetry' for perhaps more of an explanation than you would like. 'S
Poetry' is available on the internet at
http://www.seanet.com/~pburns/Spoetry or
http://www.i-way.co.uk/~pat/Spoetry 

Nick Ellis and John Lu suggested the S+ function nlminb. This function
didn't work very well in S+ 3.3 for windows (besides uses derivatives).
I haven't used it yet in S+ 5.0. 

Thank you all very much.

Alberto

--

telefone:  +351 1 3027062         fax:  +351 1 3015948

messages.subject: [S] item response models
messages.body_plain:
I have a large dataset (n c.2000) of responses on a new 34 item 
questionnaire with 5 level items.  Simple things like coefficient 
alpha, test-retest stability, convergent correlations with existing 
measures (where apt) and independence (largely) of things like 
gender and age look good as do excellent clinical/non-clinical 
differences and excellent sensitivity to change with therapy.  Now 
I'm keen to look at the items using an item response theory 
approach not least 'cos we designed it to have some "high 
anchored" and some "low anchored" items.

However, I'm rusty on this and not a professional statistician.  I did 
do some work in this area a few years back using Andrich's 
polytomous Rasch model and his DISLOC program but I suspect 
there are ways of doing things in S now that would be statistically 
and mathematically good (I suppose I mean robust and reliable!) 
and that might fairly easily spit out or provide the raw materials for 
the plots that would show what the models meant for what will be 
fairly "lay" (psychotherapists, psychiatrists and psychologists) 
audiences.

Anyone done this sort of work with S or R and want to point me to 
things I should check out?

TIA,

Chris

P.S. another largish dataset relates to a binary response measure 
so I'm also looking to pointers to binary Rasch, two and three 
parameter item response models as well as the polytomous things.

PSYCTC: Psychotherapy, Psychology, Psychiatry, Counselling
   and Therapeutic Communities; practice, research, 
   teaching and consultancy.

messages.subject: [S] Recent additions to Hmisc and Design libraries
messages.subject_clean: [S] Recent additions to Hmisc and Design libraries
messages.body_plain:
Hmisc library:
 - Added method='quantiles' to xYplot to plot for example median and quartiles 
of y
   stratified by x and other variables to get quantile bands.

- Added dataRep function - describes degree to which a new
   observation was represented in a data frame used to develop
   a predictive model

- Fixed bug in describe related to subset= in describe.formula, by
   making describe work in the usually 'method class' fashion.
  Thanks to Thomas Richards (richards at toutatis.pci.upmc.edu)
  Added Lag function

Design library:
- Changed anova.Design to print (by default) F stats and partial sums of
   squares for ols fits.  Can ask for chi-square stats using
   test='Chisq'.  Print p-values < .0001 as '<.0001' instead of 0.0000
- Added which= to print.anova.Design, to show details of hypotheses
   being tested
- Added conf.int, conf.type to predict.Design to allow C.L. for
   predicted mean or individual (for ols)
  Added se.fit to ols
- Added conf.type to plot.Design to allow plotting of C.L. for indiv.
- Added contrast function (facilitates Type II and III contrasts and
   many others)
- Added group= to predab.resample so that you can do balanced
   bootstrapping to handle k-sample problems (and to force every
   level of an ordinal response variable to be represented in every
   bootstrap sample).  This will benefit validate() and calibrate().
  Also added group= to bootcov.

The new contrast function is fairly general.  It prints estimates, confidence 
limits,
and t- or Wald test statistics and 2-sided P-values.  Here are some examples 
from
the help file (f is a fit object from ols or other Design functions):

# Compare a 30 year old female to a 40 year old male
# (with or without age x sex interaction or nonlinear age effects in the model)
contrast(f, list(sex='female', age=30), list(sex='male', age=40))

# For a model containing two treatments, centers, and treatment
# x center interaction, get 0.95 confidence intervals separately
# by center
lc <- levels(center)
contrast(f, list(treat='b', center=lc),
            list(treat='a', center=lc))

# Get 'Type III' contrast: average b - a treatment effect over
# centers, weighting centers equally (which is almost always
# an unreasonable thing to do)
contrast(f, list(treat='b', center=lc),
            list(treat='a', center=lc),
         type='average')

# Get 'Type II' contrast, weighting centers by the number of
# subjects per center.  Print the design contrast matrix used.
k <- contrast(f, list(treat='b', center=lc),
                 list(treat='a', center=lc),
              type='average', weights=table(center))
print(k, X=T)

# For a 4-treatment study, get all comparisons with control
lt <- levels(treatment)
contrast(f, list(treatment=lt[-1]),
            list(treatment=lt[ 1]),
         cnames=paste(lt[-1],lt[1],sep=':'), conf.int=1-.05/3)

# Six ways to get the same thing, for a variable that
# appears linearly in a model and does not interact with
# any other variables.  We estimate the change in y per
# unit change in a predictor x1.  Methods 4, 5 also
# provide confidence limits.  Method 6 computes nonparametric
# bootstrap confidence limits.  Methods 2-6 can work
# for models that are nonlinear or non-additive in x1.
# For that case more care is needed in choice of settings
# for x1 and the variables that interact with x1.

coef(fit)['x1']                            # method 1
diff(predict(fit, gendata(x1=c(0,1))))     # method 2
g <- Function(fit)                         # method 3
g(x1=1) - g(x1=0)
summary(fit, x1=c(0,1))                    # method 4
k <- contrast(fit, list(x1=1), list(x1=0)) # method 5
print(k, X=T)
fit <- update(fit, x=T, y=T)               # method 6
b <- bootcov(fit, B=500, coef.reps=T)
bootplot(b, X=k$X)    # bootstrap distribution and CL

Here is an example of the new print.anova.Design where the subscripts of
the regression coefficients being tested by each hypothesis are shown.

f   <- ols(y ~ treat*lsp(age,50) + rcs(bp,4))
specs(f)

ols(formula = y ~ treat * lsp(age, 50) + rcs(bp, 4))

             Assumption                  Parameters d.f. 
      treat category     a b c                      2   
        age lspline      50                         2   
         bp rcspline     103.56 116.9 123.92 135.04 3   
treat * age interaction linear x nonlinear - Ag(B)  4   

an <- anova(f, ss=F)

print(an, 'subscripts')

                                 Factor          F d.f.      P      Tested 
 treat  (Factor+Higher Order Factors)       274.90  6   <.0001 1-2,8-11   
  All Interactions                           36.96  4   <.0001 8-11       
 age  (Factor+Higher Order Factors)          48.79  6   <.0001 3-4,8-11   
  All Interactions                           36.96  4   <.0001 8-11       
  Nonlinear (Factor+Higher Order Factors)    61.27  3   <.0001 4,10-11    
 bp                                         132.10  3   <.0001 5-7        
  Nonlinear                                   0.03  2   0.9665 6-7        
 treat * age  (Factor+Higher Order Factors)  36.96  4   <.0001 8-11       
  Nonlinear                                  36.10  2   <.0001 10-11      
  Nonlinear Interaction : f(A,B) vs. AB      36.10  2   <.0001 10-11      
 TOTAL NONLINEAR                             36.90  5   <.0001 4,6-7,10-11
 TOTAL NONLINEAR + INTERACTION               37.74  7   <.0001 4,6-11     
 TOTAL                                      205.55 11   <.0001 1-11       

Error d.f.: 488 

Subscripts correspond to:
 [1] treat=b        treat=c        age            age'           bp            
 [6] bp'            bp''           treat=b * age  treat=c * age  treat=b * age'
[11] treat=c * age'

messages.subject: [S] Summary: calculation of running averages
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who responded to my question about calculation of running
averages. Here are the replies:

>>From Tim Hesterberg:

diff(cumsum(x), lag=7)

Rich Raubertas and Claude Nadeau pointed to the function filter() :

For instance filter(series,rep(1,7)/7) essentially produce 7-day
moving average.

Joel Schwartz suggested the use of ksmooth, and define the kernel to be a
box car kernel, and define the width that you want.

John Lu suggested:  You might use smooth or loess with uniform weight to do
it.     
              

Bill Dunlap included the following function and help files.
     
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bill Dunlap                                      22461 Mt Vernon-Big Lake Rd
Data Analysis Products Div. of MathSoft, Inc.    Mount Vernon, WA 98274
bill at statsci.com                                 360-428-8146

"All statements in this message represent the opinions of the author and do
not necessarily reflect MathSoft policy or position."
"running"<-
function(x, window = c(-1, 1), FUN = function(x)
sum(x)/length(x), ..., simplify = T, end.values, by = 1)
{
# applies FUN to successive overlapping subsequences of x
# val[i] <- FUN(x[(i+window[1]):(i+window[2])], ...)
# If length(window)==1, then assume user wants centered window
# with width of window (window should be odd in that case).
# E.g., window=c(-n,0) => i'th value of result depends on
# (i-n)th through i'th value of input (a realizable filter).
# The end.values argument, if supplied, will be used to fill
# in the values of the result that depend on entries of the
# input that are outside of the range of the input.  If not
# supplied, we will call FUN on a vector of the usual length
# with points off the ends filled with NA's.  (You will need
# to specify end.values only if FUN cannot handle NA's.)
        val <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(x))
        if(length(window) == 1) {
                if(window %% 2 != 1)
                        stop("length(window)==1 => centered window so width 
must be odd"
                                )
                window <- (c(-1, 1) * (window - 1))/2
        }
        if(length(window) != 2)
                stop("length(window) must be 1 or 2")
        if(diff(window) < 0)
                stop("window[1] must be less than window[2]")
        is <- seq(length = length(x), by = by)
        is <- is[is + window[1] < 1 | is + window[2] > length(x)]       
        # First take care of the endpoints, using slightly slower technique.
# We always pass the function a vector of the same length, 
# filling in points past the ends of x with NA's.
# (We do this first so that if FUN balks at NA's we stop early)
        if(missing(end.values)) {
                val[is] <- lapply(is, function(i, x, win, FUN, ...)
                {
                        tmp <- i + win
                        tmp[tmp < 1] <- NA      
        # could do tmp[tmp>length(x)] <- NA, but not needed
# as x[things>length(x)] -> NA.
                        FUN(x[tmp], ...)
                }
                , x, window[1]:window[2], FUN, ...)
        }
        else {
                val[is] <- list(end.values)
        }
        is <- setdiff(seq(length = length(x)), is)
        val[is] <- lapply(is, function(i, x, win, FUN, ...)
        {
                FUN(x[i + win], ...)
        }
        , x, window[1]:window[2], FUN, ...)
        val <- if(simplify) {
                lens <- unique(unlist(lapply(val, length)))
                if(all(lens == 1))
                        unlist(val)
                else if(length(lens) == 1)
                        t(array(unlist(val,     
        # Note this simplification is the transpose
# of that done by sapply.  This makes this
# function behave better with time series
                        recursive = F), c(lens, length(val)), list(NULL, names(
                                val))))
        }
        else val
        tsp(val) <- tsp(x)
        val
}.BG
.FN running
.TL
running statistics
.DN
Apply a function to all fixed length subsequences of a sequence
.CS
running(x, window=c(-1, 1), FUN=function(x)sum(x)/length(x), ...,
simplify=T, end.values)
.RA
.AG x
A vector of data.  It it is a time series, its time series parameters
(tsp) will be attached to the result.
.AG window
Two integers giving the endpoints of the subsequence relative to where
the value of FUN(subsequence) will be placed in the output.
In symbols, value[i] will be FUN(x[(i+window[1]):(i+window[2])]).
E.g., A 'realizible filter' will have window[2] is 0  (output does
not depend on future values of input) and a centered filter will
have window[1] being -window[2].  window[2] must not be less than window[1].
.AG FUN
A function of at least one argument.  It will be called as
FUN(x, ...), with the ... arguments being any arguments given
to running that are not in running's argument list.
.OA
.AG ...
Arguments to be passed to FUN.
.AG simplify
If FALSE, the value will be a list, with value[[i]] being the value
of FUN(x[(i+window[1]):(i+window[2])], ...).
If TRUE, running will try to coerce the list of results into a vector or
matrix.
If all results have length 1, then it will make a vector (by calling
unlist).  If all results have the same length, which is greater than 1,
then it will make a vector whose number of rows is the length of the input
and whose number of columns if the length of each output vector.
If the values have a variable length or are all length 0, then the result
is left as a list.   These rules are close to what sapply() does when
simplify is TRUE, but note that the matrix made by running is the
transpose of the one sapply would make (this is to follow the usual
structure of vector valued time series).
.AG end.values
If not supplied, the the values near the ends of the input series will
be computed as though the series were extended indefinitely with NA's
(NULL's if series is a list, ""'s if it has mode character).
If your FUN cannot deal with NA's, then supply a value here to insert
into the ends of the output.
.RT
~Describe the value returned
.DT
For linear filtering the filter, diff, and cumsum commands are
much faster.  Many filtering operations are linear, but it is
tedious to compute the coefficients; you can use running to
easily experiment and to verify the coefficients used for filter.
Running does not do autoregressive type filtering,
in which the i'th output value depends upon the local data as well as
the previously computed output values.
.SA
arima.sim, filter, diff, cumsum, sapply, lapply
.EX

> # draw line along local maxima of data
> lines(running(co2, window=c(-10,10), max))
> # draw line along local 75th percentile of data
> lines(running(co2, window=c(-10,10), quantile, .75))

Dumped

messages.body_plain:
Dear S-plusers,

My sincere thanks to Rachel Fewster, Dave Krantz, Renaud Lancelot, Julian
Stander, and Bill Venables (in alphabetical order), for their prompt reply
and their valuable advice. I have attached part of Bill Venebles' reply as
it provides the most general description to the problem:

For more general operations on rows, columns, layers, ... or an
array the more flexible tool is apply().  For these operations
you would use it as

rowsums <- function(M) apply(M, 1, sum)
colsums <- function(M) apply(M, 2, sum)

These would give almost the same answer as the above, but they
would be a little slower on large matrices, and the result would
be a vector, not a row- or column-matrix as appropriate.

> As an APL user who attempts to migrate all his APL algorithm
> into S, I presume this is one of the difficulties encountered.
> I will be grateful if the audience will kindly advise me on
> other funcitons that migrate the functions of APL atomic
> operators.

There are not many.  The arithmetic operators all behave as an
APL person would expect, but apart from that I can't think of
many.  You should get to know the functions outer(), apply(),
lapply(), sapply(), tapply() (and soon, rapply()) very well, and
think as much as possible in terms of matrix operations.  In this
respect t() and aperm() are often useful, and look up the concept
of a `matrix index' (that is, an index to an array that itself is
a matrix) - this can be exceptionally handy.  matplot() is
probably going to be useful to you as well.

Lin

messages.subject: RE: [S] Summary: routines for constrained minimisation without derivatives
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: routines for constrained minimisation without derivatives
messages.body_plain:
Alberto,

nlminb() can use derivatives but it does not require them. If you don't
give it derivatives then it calculates them by finite differences.

Nick Elis

> -----Original Message-----
> From: Alberto Murta [mailto:amurta at ipimar.pt]
> Sent: Saturday, March 20, 1999 12:31 AM
> To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu; Prof. Manuela Neves
> Subject: [S] Summary: routines for constrained minimisation without
> derivatives
> 
> 
> 
> Here is my original question:
> 
> I'm looking for a (free) Fortran routine for function minimisation
> without needing derivatives and allowing parameter constraints. This
> routine is to be integrated in a S-Plus function for a bootstrap
> procedure. I looked in Statlib and Netlib but I couldn't find any.
> 
> here are the answers I received (edited):
> 
> Matt Wiener: 
>  Take a look at: FSQP Home Page:
> http://www.isr.umd.edu/Labs/CACSE/FSQP/fsqp.html They don't 
> charge, but
> they do have some restrictions on use.  You'll have to see whether you
> find them acceptable. 
> 
> Tom Richards:
>  What about Nelder-Mead, discussed in Numerical Recipes?...(also
> suggested by Samantha Choy and Kevin Brand)
>  I don't know what type of constraints you're talking about 
> exactly, but
> if they're range constraints, you can just put in an if statement that
> says, that if the parameters go outside the permissible 
> range, then  the
> function value will be arbitrarily large.
> 
> David Mackay: 
>  Attached is a program you may find useful. This version came from
> Michael Birnbaum's web site
> http://psych.fullerton.edu/mbirnbaum/stepit.htm. There is a greatly
> expanded version of stepit but I do not have it. The expanded 
> version is
> available, for a fee, from the Quantum Chemistry Program Exchange at
> Indiana University http://qcpe5.chem.indiana.edu/qcpe.html. 
> 
> John Koval:
>  I wrote an algorithm coded in Fortran which is in the Applied
> statistics > library, known as AS319. think it is also available in
> Statlib. I wrote it in Fortran 77, but someone coded it into 
> Fortran 90.
> It definitely works without derivatives, and can be made to handle
> constraints by defining the function to have extremely large 
> values when
> > the constraints are violated - this is how I use it in one 
> of my programs. 
> 
> Max Kuhn:
>  The Nelder-Mead simplex routine code can be found in Statlib at:
> http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/apstat/47 Also, the article Olsson, D. M.
> (1774), A Sequential Simplex Program for Solving Minimization 
> Problems.
> Journal of Quality Technology, V 6, #1, pg 53 provides a Fortran
> function list, as does the book Carter, W. H., Wampler, G. L. and
> Stablein, D. L. (1983), Regression Analysis of Survival Data in Cancer
> Chemotherapy. New York : Marcell Dekker . Also, there are some
> interesting papers on this type of optimization routines (and others)
> at: http://plato.la.asu.edu/guide.html (See the section for 
> "M. Powell's
> and M. Wright's papers on Direct Search methods"). 
> 
> Patrick Burns:
>  There is already one in Splus called 'mnb0'.  See section 14.4 of 'S

> Poetry' is available on the internet at
> http://www.seanet.com/~pburns/Spoetry or
> http://www.i-way.co.uk/~pat/Spoetry 
> 
> Nick Ellis and John Lu suggested the S+ function nlminb. This function
> didn't work very well in S+ 3.3 for windows (besides uses 
> derivatives).
> I haven't used it yet in S+ 5.0. 
> 
> Thank you all very much.

messages.subject: [S] Kruskal-Wallis mutiple comparisons
messages.body_plain:
In Splus version 5 the multicomp function offers pairwise multiple comparisons
of the treatment effects from ANOVA or linear models.

I have a data set needing non parametric one way ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis).  I need
an analogous approach to identity where differences exist among the levels of
the treatment factor .  It doesn't make sense to collapse any of the treatment
effects.  No one of the treatment effects can be considered a control group.
There is no meaningful ordering of the treatment effects.

The only approach I see is to do all (n*(n-1)/2) pairwise Wilcoxon tests with a
Bonferroni adjustment of the probability value.

Any suggestions?  Any functions developed for this purpose?

Thanks

Nathan

Thanks to all who responded to my post, which is attached below
for reference.  Got lots of clever and interesting suggestions.

To briefly summarize responses:
Jack Lee suggested the functions 'hdr'

messages.body_plain:
An interesting problem. Here is one ad hoc approach that requires a bit
of exploration first but then is semiautomated. The problem as you state
it may not have a unique solution.

This is related to density estimation. As a more general approach
(instead of relying on circles) you could generate a 2-d density
function. There is software around to do kernel density estimation (e.g.
V&Rs MASS library has kde2d and there are other packages on Statlib; see
discussion on kde in this list). Once you have a density estimate, you
can find the highest density region containing 70% of the data. This
does have a unique solution. Put another way, if you contour the density
function, you just need to find that the contour that just contains 70%
of the points. I've included this in the example in case you have the
(highly recommended) MASS library. 

Good Luck,
Nick Ellis

# generate 100 data points
n<-100
set.seed(10)
dat<-data.frame(x=rnorm(n),y=rnorm(n))
# function to find number points inside circle center x radius r
n.inside.circle<-function(x,r){sum((dat$x-x[1])^2+(dat$y-x[2])^2<r^2)}

# grid of circle centres
ngrid<-10
grid<-expand.grid(x=seq(min(dat$x),max(dat$x),len=ngrid),y=seq(min(dat$y
),max(dat$y),len=ngrid))

#sequence of radii to try
r<-seq(1,2,.1) # limits found after exploration
nin<-0*r
for(i in seq(along=r)){
        
nin[i]<-max(apply(grid,1,function(x,r)n.inside.circle(x,r),r=r[i]))
}

# nin is max no. points in circle of corresponding radius; interpolate
to estimate radius of circle
# containing 70% of points
rmin<-approx(nin,r,n*0.70)$y
cat("minimum radius",rmin,"\n")

# find actual numbers of points inside circles of this radius
nin.rmin<-apply(grid,1,function(x,r)n.inside.circle(x,r),r=rmin)

# locate the point(s) for which circle of radius rmin contains maximum
number (should be close to 70)
imax<-seq(along=nin.rmin)[nin.rmin==max(nin.rmin)]

# display it all
plot(dat$x,dat$y)
for (j in imax){
        symbols(grid$x[j],grid$y[j],circles=rmin,add=T,inch=F)
        text(grid$x[j],grid$y[j],nin.rmin[j],col=2)
}

# if you have V&Rs MASS library
library(MASS)

# do kde on data
KDE<-kde2d(dat$x,dat$y)

# get density at the data points by interpolation (loess) from grid
output by kde2d
KDE.data<-cbind(expand.grid(x=KDE$x,y=KDE$y),z=as.vector(KDE$z))
dens<-predict(loess(z~x*y,data=KDE.data),dat)

# find 70th percentile from max density
dens70<-quantile(dens,1-0.70)

# plot those in highest density region
subset<-dens>dens70
sum(subset)
points(dat$x[subset],dat$y[subset],col=2)

# alternatively, show corresponding contour of density function
contour(KDE,levels=dens70,lty=2,add=T)
# contour doesn't correspond exactly with coloured points, 
# presumably due to inaccuracy of interpolation.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to
bturlach at stats.adelaide.edu.au
who suggested that I not operate on
(X'X) but rather just on X.
A reliable solution is obtained to
the longley problem.  I still can't
help but wonder, "If the LU gets 8
digits operating on X'X, why can't
QR or SVD beat that?"

Anyhow, in the previously posted code,
which seeks a solution to b = Ax where
A is the data matrix,
change the definitions of A and b as
follows:

A <- as.Matrix(longley.dat)
b <- y

Eliminate all references to LU decomposition, since 
LU doesn't work on rectangular matrices. The following output
is achieved.

I also pulled down LAPACK from netlib
and used their QR routine (don't have
time to do the SVD).

Number of Accurate Digits for
Each of Seven Longley Coefficients
> print(fred, digits = 3)
    QR  SVD  LAPACK
1 12.2 12.2    12.9
2 10.9 11.0    11.6
3 11.8 11.8    12.5
4 12.6 12.5    13.2
5 13.2 13.1    14.0
6 11.6 11.8    12.3
7 12.2 12.3    12.9

On a curious note,

S-PLUS has the Matrix library.  The on-line
documentation notes that the commands
qr() and qr.Matrix() are not the same thing
and are not interchangeable.

So I abandoned the Matrix Library and
attempted to solve the problem using
the built-in (non-library) functions.

  A.qrd <- qr.Matrix(A)
 A.sqrd <- qr(A)

So I tried to use the built-in command to solve the
longley problem and got

> qr.fitted(A.sqrd,y)
Error in qr.fitted(A.sqrd, y): First argument should be a qr object
Dumped

So I checked the class of my qr object
> class(A.sqrd)
[1] "qr.Matrix" "decomp"  

which is curious, and I also checked the class of the
analagous quantity computed by the library Matrix

> class(A.qrd)
[1] "qr.Matrix" "decomp"   

Hmmm.  This gets more and more curious.
Why is qr object of class Matrix?

Bruce

messages.subject: [S] Kruskal-Wallis multiple comparisons
messages.body_plain:
I sent a query to S-News about functions for multiple comparison testing after a
Kruskal-Wallis test is significant.

Thanks to those who contributed responses:

Ken Butler butler at mscs.dal.ca

As I understand it, Kruskal-Wallis is "equivalent" to an ordinary one-way
ANOVA that uses the ranks instead of the original data. (K-W produces a
chi-squared statistic compared to ANOVA's F, but these would give
identical P-values for infinitely large samples and can be expected to be
close on actual data sets.)

So my approach here would first of all be to add a column containing the
ranks of y to my data set and run a "fake" Kruskal-Wallis using lm with
with my ranks-of-y as the dependent variable. Provided that this agreed
closely in P-value with my "real" Kruskal-Wallis, I'd then use multicomp,
again with the ranks-of-y as my dependent variable.

It would presumably be better to use a multiple comparison procedure
geared to ranks (rather than pretending that the ranks are normally
distributed, which is really what is happening here). I wouldn't be at all
surprised if such a procedure exists, but I don't know of one.

Franz J. Mueter mueter at ims.alaska.edu

A while ago I modified the kruskal.test() function to include multiple
comparisons. The output includes a simple matrix of pairwise comparisons (only
if the overall test rejects null hypothesis), where T indicates the difference
is significant at the given level of alpha. The test is based on a multiple
comparison test given in:

Conover, W.J. (1980) Practical Nonparametric statistics. 2nd edition. p. 231

The modified kruskal test follows:

"kruskal"<-
function(y, groups, alpha = 0.05)
{
# modified from kruskal.test by Franz Mueter, 9/13/96
# computes Kruskal-Wallis test statistic and p-value (assuming Chi-square
# distribution), as well as all pairwise comparisons at the specified
# level alpha (T if Null hypothesis is rejected).
        groups <- unclass(groups)
        if(any(!is.finite(groups)))
                stop("NA's/Inf's not allowed in 'groups'.")
        groups <- as.category(groups)
        if(length(y) != length(groups))
                stop("'y' and 'groups' must have the same length.")
        if(!all(y.ok <- is.number(y))) {
                is.not.number.warning(y)
                y <- y[y.ok]
                groups <- groups[y.ok]
                warning(paste(sum(!y.ok),
                        "observations (y[i], groups[i]) with NA in 'y'
removed."
                        ))
        }
        N <- sum(grp.sizes <- table(groups))
        S.2 <- 1/(N - 1) * (sum(rank(y)^2) - N/4 * (N + 1)^2)
        R <- tapply(rank(y), groups, sum)
        K <- 1/S.2 * (sum(R^2/grp.sizes) - N/4 * (N + 1)^2)
        ret.val <- list(statistic = K, parameters = length(grp.sizes) - 1,
                alternative = "two.sided", method =
                "Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test", data.name = paste(deparse(
                substitute(y)), " and ", deparse(substitute(groups)), sep =
"")
                )
        ret.val$p.value <- 1 - pchisq(ret.val$statistic, ret.val$parameters)
        names(ret.val$statistic) <- "Kruskal-Wallis chi-square"
        names(ret.val$parameters) <- "df"
        ret.val <- ret.val[c("statistic", "parameters", "p.value",
                "alternative", "method", "data.name")]
        number.of.observations <- table(as.category(groups))
        grps <- length(grp.sizes)
        group.medians <- round(tapply(y, groups, median), 3)
        names(group.medians) <- names(table(groups))
        if(ret.val$p.value < alpha) {
                Mult <- qt(1 - alpha/2, N - grps) * sqrt((S.2 *
                        (N - 1 - K))/(N - grps))
                LHS <- abs(rep((R/grp.sizes), rep(grps, grps)) - rep((R/
                        grp.sizes), grps))
                RHS <- Mult * sqrt(rep((1/grp.sizes), rep(grps, grps))
                        + rep((1/grp.sizes), grps))
                pairwise.comparisons <- matrix(LHS > RHS, nrow = grps,
                        dimnames = list(names(table(groups)),
                        names(table(groups))))
        }
        attr(ret.val, "class") <- "htest"
        return(number.of.observations, group.medians, ret.val, if(ret.val$
                p.value < alpha) pairwise.comparisons)
}

Don MacQueen macq at llnl.gov

The book
  Simultaneous Statistical Inference by Rupert G. Miller
has a chapter on this.
2nd ed., Springer Verlag, 1981
ISBN 0-387-90548-0

Lorenz Gygax LGygax at amath.unizh.ch

Look e.g. into:

AUTHOR = {Zar, J L},
TITLE = {Biostatistical Analysis},
PUBLISHER = {Prentice Hall},
YEAR = {1984},
ADDRESS = {NJ},

he proposes an equivalent to the parametric multicomparison test for the
KW. As I remember it, it should be easy to implement (or even calculate by
hand) and I have never seen it implemented.

--

messages.subject: [S] Re: Data Format
messages.body_plain:
There was considerable interest by other members of our group in answers to  
my question about data format. So, I will summarize the helpful suggestions  
that I received.

My original question was:

> Hi,
>
> I have data
>
> 1/1/99  80
> 1/1/99  85
> 1/1/99  83
> 1/1/99  84
> 1/2/99  80
> 1/2/99  78
> 1/2/99  73
> 1/2/99  81
>
> I want to write it as follows
>
> 1/1/99  80      85      83      84
> 1/2/99  80      78      73      81
>
> I would appreciate it if somebody could help me.
*****************************************************************
Renaud Lancelot:

Assuming:

1. your data are in a data frame,
2. you don't have any missing value,
3. Your data are ordered by date,

the following should do what you need:

> test <- data.frame(date = dates(c(rep("1/1/99", 4), rep("2/2/99", 4)),  
format = "dd/mm/y"), x = c(80, 85, 83,
        84, 80, 78, 73, 81))
***********************************************************
Andrew Sinclair:

Something like

t(sapply(tapply(vals, idx, function(x) x)))

where vals are your values and idx is your vector of names.
***************************************************************
Peter Alspach:

If your data is in ahmed, then

> classes <- summary(ahmed[,1])
> t(matrix(ahmed[,2], classes[1], length(classes)))

will give

        80      85      83      84
        80      78      73      81

The classnames can be added as well .....
********************************************************
Nick Ellis

> dat
      V1 V2
1 1/1/99 80
2 1/1/99 85
3 1/1/99 83
4 1/1/99 84
5 1/2/99 80
6 1/2/99 78
7 1/2/99 73
8 1/2/99 81
> dat1<-as.data.frame(t(as.data.frame(tapply(dat[,2],dat[,1],c))))
> dat1<-cbind(date=row.names(dat1),dat1)

***************************************************************

Also

Nicholas Barrowman suggested that a PERL script could easily do it.
Enayet Talukder suggested that I should consult the S+ helpguide on matrix.

***************************************************************************
Thanks a lot. I appreciate all your help.
